title: Is Using AI Every Day Making You Worse at Thinking?
meta_title: Is Using AI Every Day Making You Worse at Thinking? | Aperture
summary: Daily AI use can reduce critical thinking and recall, per a 2026 MIT study. Here's which tasks are safe to offload and which to protect.
primary_question: Does using AI every day make you worse at critical thinking?

content:
The research is worth paying attention to. A 2026 MIT study tracked brain activity in 54 participants writing essays, and the ChatGPT group showed lower neural engagement across all 32 measured brain regions than those writing unaided. Some networks showed up to 55% weaker activity. Daily AI use does appear to reduce certain kinds of cognitive effort. The practical question is which tasks you can safely hand off and which you genuinely shouldn't.

Key Takeaways

  • A 2026 MIT EEG study found AI-assisted writers showed up to 55% weaker neural activity than unaided writers
  • 83% of AI-heavy users couldn't recall key points from essays they had just written with AI help
  • The cognitive hit is worst for inference and original writing, not for repetitive or lookup tasks
  • The problem isn't how much AI you use but which cognitive tasks you hand off
  • Indian students preparing for JEE, CAT, or UPSC face direct risk from outsourcing daily reasoning practice to AI

What Did the MIT Brain Study Actually Find?

The MIT 2026 EEG study had 54 participants write essays in three conditions: unaided, using Google Search, or using ChatGPT. The ChatGPT group showed the lowest neural engagement of all three groups. Up to 55% weaker neural coupling was measured in some regions, and 83% of AI users couldn't recall key points from their own just-written essays.

The study design was simple but the pattern was striking. Researchers asked all participants to recall their essay's key points after each session. Most unaided writers managed it well enough. Most ChatGPT users drew a near-blank. They had produced an essay, but their brains hadn't engaged with the material deeply enough to recieve it into memory.

When researchers swapped conditions and made previous AI users write unaided, those participants showed lingering deficits in the same session. The researchers describe the effect as "acute cognitive offloading" rather than permanent damage, and the study hasn't been peer-reviewed yet. Still, the pattern matches APA's 2026 review of how AI is reshaping human thinking.

Which AI Tasks Are Actually Safe to Delegate?

Formatting and proofreading already-written text are generally safe to offload, and so are fact lookups and boilerplate templates. The higher-risk tasks are first drafts and evaluating whether a claim holds up. Those build the kind of reasoning you want to keep, and they take the biggest hit when you hand them off consistently.

Safe to Delegate to AIProtect as Human-Only
Formatting and restructuring drafts you've writtenFirst drafts and original arguments
Looking up facts, definitions, and datesEvaluating whether a claim is actually true
Generating boilerplate emails and templatesWriting where your voice or judgment matters
Summarizing documents you've already readMaking sense of complex material you need to retain
Language polishing and translationForming your own take on ambiguous data

The seperate categories matter more the heavier your AI use gets. It's not about the tool itself. It's about which mental moves you keep making yourself, because those are the ones that stay sharp.

Does AI Use Affect Indian Students and Professionals More?

Probably yes, for a specific reason. Indian students are among the heaviest AI users globally, and for many, AI fills a real language fluency gap. But using AI to handle the reasoning in English writing because English is already hard means skipping the practice that would make them better at both.

For students preparing for JEE Advanced, CAT, or UPSC, this is direct. These exams test inference and analytical writing under pressure. Neither ability gets sharper if you outsource the daily practice to a chatbot. Checking grammar after you've written something is a very different matter from asking AI to draft the thinking for you.

A recent ResearchGate study on AI tool dependency in Indian higher education found that students reported reduced confidence when completing tasks without AI help. That discomfort is the signal. When an unassisted task starts to feel foreign, the dependency has gone past convenience into something worth managing.

How Do You Use AI Without Losing Your Thinking Skills?

Write your first draft before opening any AI tool. Use AI to look things up, not to figure them out for you. The reasoning stays in your hands that way, and the polish is what gets offloaded.

  • Write your first draft before touching AI. Even a rough one. Then use AI to improve what you've already created. The inferencing stays yours.
  • Read AI output critically, not passively. Skim the source yourself and push back when something feels off. That skeptical reflex is definately worth preserving.
  • Set one task per day you complete without AI help. A paragraph or a decision. Consistency matters more than scale.
  • Try the swap test occasionally: do something you'd normally hand to AI. If it feels impossibly hard, that's useful information about where your dependency has drifted.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does using ChatGPT every day reduce your intelligence?

Not permanently, based on current evidence. The 2026 MIT study found acute cognitive offloading, meaning lower brain engagement during AI tasks, but describes the effects as reversible rather than permanent damage. The real risk is gradual skill atrophy if you stop practicing inference and original writing on your own over time.

Which AI tasks are safe for students preparing for competitive exams?

Formatting and proofreading text you have already written are low-risk, and so is vocabulary lookup. The higher-risk uses are generating first drafts and deciding whether arguments hold up. For JEE, CAT, or UPSC preparation, those are precisely the skills being tested, so protecting them as human-only tasks is worth the inconvenience.

Does AI use affect memory?

Yes, in the short term. The MIT 2026 EEG study found that 83% of AI-heavy users could not recall key points from essays they had just written with AI help. Writing or reasoning through something yourself produces stronger memory encoding. When AI handles the generative work, your brain skips the consolidation that would normally make the content stick.

Can you use AI heavily and still keep your critical thinking sharp?

Yes, with deliberate task selection. The research suggests the problem is which tasks you hand off, not total volume. People who use AI for formatting and routine lookup while keeping inference and first-draft writing as human tasks appear to avoid the deficits the studies identify. The difference is between using AI to produce and using it to improve.

Is the MIT AI brain-activity study peer-reviewed?

Not yet, as of mid-2026. The researchers describe their findings as evidence of acute cognitive offloading rather than permanent harm. The study may be revised after review, and the specific figures should be treated as preliminary. Still, the pattern is consistent with earlier work on cognitive dependency, and the practical guidance holds regardless of the final status.

The Short Version

The 2026 MIT brain-activity data is worth taking seriously, caveats and all. When AI handles the thinking work, your brain skips it, and the skipping shows up in recall and cognitive engagement within the same session. The fix isn't to quit AI. It's to keep inference and original drafting in your own hands. The formatting and boilerplate? Hand those off freely.
